intro: Look around your home and your street. You might eat food from Mexico, wear shoes made in Vietnam and hear a song from Nigeria. People all over the world are connected. This unit helps you see how.

First, you will learn what culture is. Culture is the shared way of life of a group: its language, food, beliefs, art and manners. You will see how people learn culture, and how cultures meet and mix. Then you will take a tour of Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas.

By the end, you will be able to name the continents and read a map. You will be able to describe life in four regions. You will also be able to talk about other cultures with respect, and without stereotypes.
bigQuestion: What makes each culture special, and what do people all over the world share?

title: Continents and Cultures

chapters.title: What Is Culture?
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the shared ways of a group shape the way people live, and how do those ways change?

story.title: Marco's Kitchen List
story.kicker: A boy in Chicago goes looking for the world and finds it in his own home.
paragraphs: Marco lives in an apartment in Chicago. One rainy Saturday, his teacher's homework seemed strange. Make a list of things in your home that came from another country. Marco grabbed a pencil and a notebook. He started in the kitchen.

The rice bag said it came from Thailand. The bananas had a sticker from Guatemala. His grandmother's tortilla press came from Mexico, where she grew up. The teapot was a gift from a neighbor who moved from China. Marco's list was getting long fast.

In the living room he found more. His sister's soccer ball was made in Pakistan. The TV was built in South Korea. A drum on the shelf came from Ghana. His dad had bought it at a street fair on the South Side. Even the word pajamas came from a language of South Asia.

Marco counted. He had found things from eleven countries on five continents. He thought about it. His family ate tamales and fried rice. They watched soccer and baseball. They spoke English and Spanish. Maybe his home was not just one culture. Maybe it was many, mixed together.
story.think: What is one thing in your home, like food, music or a word, that came from another place?

sections.title: The Shared Ways of a Group

lessons.title: What Culture Means
lessons.mainIdea: Culture is the shared way of life of a group of people.
reading: Think about how your family eats dinner. Do you use forks, chopsticks or your hands? Do you eat at a table or on the floor? Families in different places answer these questions in different ways.

These shared ways are called *culture*. Culture is the way of life a group of people shares. It includes language, food, clothing and beliefs. It also includes art, music, stories, holidays and manners.

Every group has a culture. A country has one. A town can have one. Even a school has its own ways, like its songs and rules. A *custom* is one habit that a group shares, like shaking hands to say hello.

words.d: the way of life a group of people shares, like its language, food, beliefs and art
a habit or way of doing something that a group shares

look.title: Two Ways to Say Hello
look.text: In the United States, many people shake hands when they meet. In Japan, many people bow. They bend forward from the waist. Both actions mean the same thing: hello, and I respect you.
look.prompt: What is one custom your family or school uses to greet people?

check.q: What is culture?
choices: The shared way of life of a group
check.why: Culture is the way of life a group shares, including language, food, beliefs, art and more.

check.q: Which of these is part of culture?
check.why: Music is part of culture. Mountains, wind and oceans are parts of nature.

check.q: Bowing to say hello in Japan is an example of a...
check.why: A custom is a habit a group shares, like bowing or shaking hands.

lessons.title: Language, Food and Clothing
lessons.mainIdea: Language, food and clothing are three parts of culture you can hear, taste and see.
reading: Walk down a busy street in Chicago. You might hear English, Spanish, Polish and Arabic. Each *language* is a way people share ideas with words. Around the world, people speak about 7,000 languages.

Food is part of culture too. In Mexico, corn tortillas are a daily food. In Japan, rice is served with many meals. In Ethiopia, people share a flat bread called injera. Families pass their recipes down from grandparents to grandchildren.

Clothing shows culture as well. In Scotland, some people wear a kilt on special days. In India, many women wear a long cloth called a sari. A piece of clothing that is part of a group's history is called *traditional* clothing.

words.d: a system of words that people use to speak, write and share ideas
passed down from older people to younger people over a long time

look.title: Languages Spoken in Each Region
look.cite: Ethnologue: Languages of the World, SIL International, 2023
look.prompt: Which region has the most languages? Which has the fewest?

check.q: About how many languages do people speak in the world?
check.why: The reading says people speak about 7,000 languages around the world.

check.q: Injera is a flat bread shared in which country?
check.why: The reading says people in Ethiopia share a flat bread called injera.

check.q: What does traditional mean?
choices: Passed down over a long time
check.why: Traditional means passed down from older people to younger people over a long time.

lessons.title: Beliefs, Art and Holidays
lessons.mainIdea: Beliefs, art, stories and holidays show what a group thinks is important.
reading: Every year, many families in Mexico celebrate the Day of the Dead. They build a small table called an ofrenda. They put photos, flowers and favorite foods on it. The holiday is a loving way to remember family members who have died.

Holidays often come from *beliefs*. A belief is an idea a person holds to be true, like a religious teaching. Christians celebrate Christmas. Jews celebrate Passover. Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr. Hindus celebrate Diwali, a festival of lights.
Art and stories carry culture too. Groups tell old stories called folktales. They teach lessons, like being brave or kind. Painting, dance, weaving and music help people remember who they are.

words.d: an idea a person holds to be true, such as a religious teaching
an old story told by a group of people, often to teach a lesson
a special day when people celebrate or remember something

look.title: A Right to Culture
look.text: Everyone has the right freely to participate in the cultural life of the community, to enjoy the arts and to share in scientific advancement and its benefits.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 27, 1948
look.prompt: In your own words, what does this sentence say every person can do?

check.q: What do families put on an ofrenda for the Day of the Dead?
check.why: The reading says families put photos, flowers and favorite foods on the ofrenda.

check.q: Which holiday is a Hindu festival of lights?
check.why: The reading names Diwali as the Hindu festival of lights.

check.q: What is a folktale?
choices: An old story that often teaches a lesson
check.why: A folktale is an old story told by a group, often to teach a lesson.

lessons.title: We Learn Our Culture
lessons.mainIdea: People are not born knowing their culture; they learn it from family, friends and school.
reading: A baby is not born knowing how to say thank you. She learns it. Her parents say it again and again. Soon she says it too. Culture works this way. People learn it by watching and listening.

Families teach songs, recipes and manners. Schools teach a country's history and holidays. Friends teach games and jokes. Places of worship teach beliefs. Learning the ways of your group is called growing up in a culture.

Because culture is learned, anyone can learn about another culture. A child who moves to a new country can learn a new language. A family can learn to cook a new food. People can hold on to their own culture and learn a new one too.

words.d: gained by watching, listening, practicing or being taught
polite ways of acting that a group expects, like saying please and thank you

look.title: Grandma's Recipe
look.text: Ana stands next to her grandmother in the kitchen. Grandma does not use a written recipe. She says, watch my hands. Ana watches her fold the dough. Next year, Ana folds it herself.
look.prompt: How is Ana learning her culture? Name two ways.

check.q: How do people get their culture?
choices: They find it on a map
They buy it at a store
check.why: Culture is learned by watching, listening and being taught by family, friends and school.

check.q: Who teaches Ana to make the dough?
check.why: In the story, Ana learns by watching her grandmother's hands.

check.q: What can a child who moves to a new country do?
choices: Learn a new culture and keep the old one
check.why: The reading says people can hold on to their own culture and learn a new one too.

lessons.title: Cultures Meet and Mix
lessons.mainIdea: When people move and trade, their cultures meet, mix and change.
reading: Chicago is famous for deep-dish pizza. But pizza first came from Italy. Italian families brought it to America. Then cooks in Chicago made a new kind in a deep pan. A food from one place changed in a new place.

The same thing happens with other foods. Tacos came from Mexico. Ramen noodle soup is popular in Japan, and its roots go back to China. Today you can eat all three in Chicago. When cultures meet and share, this is called *cultural exchange*.

People often move to a new country for work, for family or for safety. A person who moves to live in a new country is an *immigrant*. Immigrants bring their foods, words and music. Over time, these become part of the new place too.

words.d: when groups share and trade ideas, foods, words and art
a person who moves to live in a new country

look.title: One Street, Many Kitchens
look.text: Picture one block in Chicago. There is a taqueria, a Polish bakery, a Chinese noodle shop and an Italian pizza place. Neighbors from all four shops eat lunch at each other's counters.
look.prompt: How does this one block show cultures meeting and mixing?

check.q: Where did pizza first come from?
check.why: The reading says pizza first came from Italy, and Chicago cooks later made deep-dish pizza.

check.q: What is an immigrant?
choices: A person who moves to live in a new country
A person who never leaves home
check.why: An immigrant is a person who moves to live in a new country.

check.q: Ramen from Japan with roots in China is an example of...
check.why: Cultural exchange is when groups share and trade foods and ideas, as ramen shows.

lessons.title: Words That Traveled
lessons.mainIdea: Languages borrow words from each other, so English is full of words from around the world.
reading: Say these words out loud: ketchup, pajamas, tomato, safari. They all sound like English. But each one came from another language. Words travel when people travel.

Pajamas comes from languages of South Asia. Tomato comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs in Mexico. Safari comes from Swahili, a language of East Africa. A word that one language takes from another is called a *loanword*.

Chicago's own name has a story too. It comes from a word in a Native American language of the area. Many people say it named a wild onion or garlic plant that grew near the river. Place names often hold a piece of history.

words.d: a word that one language takes from another language
a language spoken by many people in East Africa

look.title: Words on a Grocery List
look.text: A shopping list says: tomatoes, chocolate, coffee, ketchup and shampoo. Tomato and chocolate came from Nahuatl in Mexico. Coffee came through Arabic and Turkish. Shampoo came from Hindi in India. One list holds words from four corners of the world.
look.prompt: Pick one word from the list. Where did it come from, and how might it have traveled?

check.q: What is a loanword?
choices: A word taken from another language
A word only used at school
check.why: A loanword is a word one language takes from another.

check.q: The word tomato comes from which language?
check.why: The reading says tomato comes from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.

check.q: Safari comes from a language of which place?
check.why: Safari comes from Swahili, a language of East Africa.

lessons.title: The Seven Continents
lessons.mainIdea: Most maps in U.S. schools show seven continents, but some countries count five or six.
reading: Look at a world map. You will see big pieces of land with ocean around them. A very large piece of land is called a *continent*. Most U.S. schools teach seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America.

Not everyone counts the same way. In many Latin American countries, students learn that North and South America are one continent, called America. Some count Europe and Asia as one, called Eurasia. So some people count six continents, and some count five.
Asia is the largest continent. Australia is the smallest. Antarctica is covered in ice, and no one lives there all year. Scientists visit and stay there for months at a time to do research.

words.d: one of the very large pieces of land on Earth
the icy continent at the South Pole, where no one lives all year

look.title: How Big Is Each Continent?
look.cite: National Geographic Society, continent facts; common rounded estimates
look.prompt: Which continent is the largest? About how many times bigger is Asia than Europe?

check.q: Which continent is the largest?
check.why: The reading and the chart show Asia is the largest continent.

check.q: Why do some students learn about six continents?
choices: They count North and South America as one
check.why: In many Latin American countries, North and South America are counted as one continent, America.

check.q: Which continent has no people living there all year?
check.why: Antarctica is covered in ice, and people only stay for a time to do research.

lessons.title: Maps and Globes
lessons.mainIdea: A globe shows Earth's true shape, and a flat map is easier to carry but stretches some places.
reading: Spin a globe in your classroom. It is round like Earth. A *globe* is a model of Earth shaped like a ball. It shows the sizes and shapes of land and water most truly.

A *map* is a flat drawing of a place. You can fold it and carry it. But Earth is round, so a flat map must stretch some parts. On many world maps, Greenland looks as big as Africa. Really, Africa is about 14 times larger.

Maps have helpful tools. A compass rose shows north, south, east and west. A key explains the symbols. The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth. It splits the world into a north half and a south half.

words.d: a round model of Earth
a flat drawing that shows where places are
an imaginary line around the middle of Earth

look.title: Peel an Orange
look.text: Try peeling an orange in one piece. Now try to press the peel flat on a table. It tears and stretches. Mapmakers have the same problem when they turn round Earth into a flat map.
look.prompt: Why does a flat map always change the shapes or sizes of some places a little?

check.q: What is a globe?
choices: A flat drawing of a city
check.why: A globe is a round model of Earth that shows sizes and shapes most truly.

check.q: On many flat maps, Greenland looks as big as Africa. What is true?
check.why: The reading says Africa is really about 14 times larger than Greenland.

check.q: What does the equator do?
choices: Shows the symbols on a map
Splits Earth into north and south halves
check.why: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle that splits Earth into north and south halves.

lessons.title: Respect Without Stereotypes
lessons.mainIdea: People in one country are not all alike, so we learn about each person instead of guessing.
reading: Imagine someone said, everyone from Chicago loves deep-dish pizza. Is that true? Some Chicagoans love it. Some never eat it. Some cannot eat cheese. One sentence cannot describe millions of people.

A *stereotype* is an idea that all people in a group are the same. Stereotypes are unfair because people are different. In any country, people live in cities and on farms. They have different jobs, beliefs and favorite foods.

*Respect* means treating people and their ways with care. When you meet someone from another culture, you can ask and listen. You can say, tell me about your family's holidays. Then you learn about a real person, not a guess.

words.d: an unfair idea that all people in a group are the same
treating people and their ways with care and kindness

look.title: Two Students From Brazil
look.text: Lucas and Julia both come from Brazil. Lucas grew up in Sao Paulo, a huge city, and loves video games. Julia grew up on a farm near a river and loves to fish. They both speak Portuguese. They both cheer for Brazil in soccer.
look.prompt: What do Lucas and Julia share? How are they different?

check.q: What is a stereotype?
choices: A true fact about one person
An idea that all people in a group are the same
check.why: A stereotype is an unfair idea that all people in a group are the same.

check.q: What do Lucas and Julia both speak?
check.why: The passage says they both speak Portuguese, the main language of Brazil.

check.q: What is a respectful way to learn about someone's culture?
choices: Assume they are like everyone else
check.why: The reading says you can ask and listen, so you learn about a real person.

review.q: Which list shows parts of culture?
review.why: Culture includes language, food, clothing, beliefs, art, music, stories, holidays and manners.

review.q: In Marco's story, what did he find in his home?
review.why: Marco found things from eleven countries on five continents.
Culture is learned from family, friends, school and places of worship.

review.q: Deep-dish pizza in Chicago shows that cultures...
review.why: Pizza came from Italy and changed into a new kind in Chicago.

review.q: What does a compass rose on a map show?
review.why: A compass rose shows the four directions.

review.q: Which is a loanword in English?
review.why: Safari came into English from Swahili, a language of East Africa.

choices: Everyone in Brazil lives on a farm
People in one country are all alike
People in one country can be very different
review.why: People in any country have different jobs, homes, beliefs and tastes.

review.q: Why is a globe more accurate than a flat map?
review.why: A globe is round like Earth, so it does not have to stretch places the way a flat map does.

chapters.title: A Tour of Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas
chapters.bigQuestion: What makes each part of the world special, and what do people everywhere share?

story.title: Four Pen Pals, One Saturday
story.kicker: Four kids on four continents write about the very same day.
paragraphs: Ms. Rivera's class in Chicago has pen pals around the world. This month, each pen pal wrote about the same Saturday. The letters came by email. The class read them out loud, one by one.

Sofia lives in Krakow, Poland. On Saturday she walked with her dad past an old castle on a hill. They bought warm pretzel rings from a street cart. In the evening she practiced piano for a school concert.

Arjun lives in Mumbai, India. His city is crowded and full of sound. On Saturday he played cricket in a lane with his cousins. At night the family ate dal and rice. His grandmother told an old story about a clever monkey.

Amina lives in Dakar, Senegal, on the coast of West Africa. On Saturday she went to the market with her aunt to buy fish. At home they cooked thieboudienne, a dish of fish and rice. Her brother drummed while the rice cooked.

Diego lives in Cusco, Peru, high in the Andes Mountains. His grandparents speak Quechua and Spanish. On Saturday he helped them sell woven blankets at a market. The class noticed something. All four kids spent the day with family and food.
story.think: The four pen pals live far apart. What is one way their Saturdays were alike, and one way they were different?

lessons.title: Many Countries Close Together
lessons.mainIdea: Europe is a small continent with many countries and many languages close together.
reading: In Europe, you can ride a train for a few hours and cross into another country. Europe is one of the smallest continents. But it has more than 40 countries packed close together.

Each country has its own language, or even several. People speak French in France and German in Germany. They speak Polish in Poland and Italian in Italy. Many Europeans learn two or three languages in school.

Many European countries work together in a group called the *European Union*. Many of its members use the same money, called the euro. A *border* is a line where one country ends and another begins. Inside much of the European Union, people cross borders without stopping.

words.d: a line where one country ends and another begins
a group of European countries that work together and trade freely

look.title: The European Union's Motto
look.text: The European Union's motto says its members are united in diversity. They work together, while keeping their own languages and cultures.
look.prompt: What does it mean to be united and different at the same time?

check.q: Why can you reach another country quickly by train in Europe?
choices: Europe has many countries close together
check.why: The reading says Europe is small and has more than 40 countries packed close together.

check.q: What money do many European Union members share?
check.why: The reading says many members of the European Union use the euro.

check.q: What is a border?
choices: A line where one country ends and another begins
check.why: A border is the line where one country ends and another begins.

lessons.title: Old Castles and New Cities
lessons.mainIdea: In Europe, very old buildings stand next to modern cities.
reading: In Sofia's city of Krakow, Wawel Castle sits on a hill above the river. Polish kings lived there hundreds of years ago. Today, families visit it on weekends, and new apartments and shops stand nearby.

Much of Europe looks like this. Rome has ruins from ancient Rome, about 2,000 years old. Paris has the Eiffel Tower, built in 1889. London has old churches and new glass towers. A place people protect because it shows the past is a *historic site*.
Europe's past is not only castles. Wars, including two world wars, did great harm there. After World War II, many countries chose to trade and work together. They hoped this would help keep peace.

words.d: a place people protect because it shows something important from the past
what is left of old buildings that have fallen apart

look.title: Sofia's Walk Home
look.text: Sofia walks past a stone castle wall that is hundreds of years old. Then she passes a coffee shop with Wi-Fi and a bus stop with a digital sign. Old and new sit side by side on one street.
look.prompt: Why might a city keep its old buildings instead of tearing them down?

check.q: What sits on a hill above the river in Krakow?
check.why: The reading says Wawel Castle, where Polish kings lived, sits on a hill in Krakow.

check.q: When was the Eiffel Tower built?
check.why: The reading says the Eiffel Tower in Paris was built in 1889.

check.q: After World War II, many European countries chose to...
check.why: The reading says they chose to trade and work together, hoping to help keep peace.

lessons.title: The Largest Continent
lessons.mainIdea: Asia is the biggest continent, and more than half of the world's people live there.
reading: Asia stretches from the icy north of Russia to the warm islands of Indonesia. It holds the tallest mountain on Earth, Mount Everest. It holds wide deserts, thick rain forests and huge cities.

Asia is the largest continent by land. It also has the most people. About 4.7 billion people live in Asia. That is close to 6 out of every 10 people on Earth. A count of how many people live in a place is its *population*.

Many of the world's oldest *civilizations* began in Asia. A civilization is a large group with cities, leaders and writing. China, India and the land between two rivers called Mesopotamia all had early civilizations.

words.d: the number of people who live in a place
a large society with cities, leaders, jobs and often writing

look.title: Where the World's People Live
look.cite: United Nations, World Population Prospects, 2022 revision
look.prompt: Which region has the most people? How many more billions than Africa?

check.q: Which mountain in Asia is the tallest on Earth?
check.why: The reading says Asia holds Mount Everest, the tallest mountain on Earth.

check.q: About how many people live in Asia?
check.why: The reading and the chart say about 4.7 billion people live in Asia.

check.q: What is population?
choices: The number of people in a place
check.why: Population is the number of people who live in a place.

lessons.title: China and India
lessons.mainIdea: China and India each have more than a billion people and very old, rich cultures.
reading: China and India are neighbors, with the high Himalaya Mountains between them. Each has more than 1.4 billion people. In 2023, India passed China to become the country with the most people.

China's civilization is thousands of years old. Most people speak Mandarin Chinese. Chinese writing uses characters, and each one stands for a word or part of a word. Families gather for the Lunar New Year, often called Spring Festival.

India has many languages. Hindi and English are used by the national government, and the country officially recognizes 22 languages. Many faiths live side by side there, including Hinduism, Islam, Sikhism, Christianity and Buddhism. India is a *democracy*, where people vote for their leaders.

words.d: the most widely spoken form of Chinese
a written sign in Chinese that stands for a word or part of a word
a government where people vote to choose their leaders

look.title: Countries With the Most People
look.cite: United Nations, World Population Prospects, 2022 revision
look.prompt: About how many times more people live in India than in the United States?

check.q: Which mountains lie between China and India?
check.why: The reading says the high Himalaya Mountains are between China and India.

check.q: In 2023, which country passed China in population?
check.why: The reading says India passed China in 2023 to have the most people.

check.q: How many languages does India officially recognize?
check.why: The reading says India officially recognizes 22 languages.

lessons.title: A Day With Arjun's Family
lessons.mainIdea: In a big Asian city, family, food and play shape a child's everyday life.
reading: Arjun wakes up in Mumbai, a city of millions on India's west coast. His family lives in an apartment with his grandparents. Several generations under one roof is common in India. This is called an *extended family*.

Arjun's mother takes a crowded commuter train to work. Arjun goes to school, where he studies in English and in Marathi, the language of his state. After school he plays cricket, a bat-and-ball game loved across India.

At dinner the family eats dal, a stew of lentils, with rice and flat bread. Some families in Mumbai eat with their right hand. Arjun's grandmother tells stories from the Panchatantra, a very old collection of animal fables from India.

words.d: a family that includes grandparents, aunts, uncles or cousins living together or close by
a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson

look.title: The Clever Monkey
look.text: In one old Panchatantra tale, a crocodile tricks a monkey into riding on his back. Out in the river, the crocodile says he wants the monkey's heart. The monkey says he left his heart in the tree. The crocodile swims back, and the monkey escapes.
look.prompt: What lesson could this fable teach a child?

check.q: What is an extended family?
choices: A family with only one child

lessons.title: Deserts, Rivers and 54 Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Africa is a huge continent with 54 countries, the Sahara Desert and the Nile River.
reading: Africa is the second largest continent. It has 54 countries, more than any other continent. People there speak well over 1,000 languages. Arabic, Swahili, Hausa, Yoruba and Amharic are just a few.

Africa has the largest hot desert in the world, the *Sahara*. It covers much of North Africa and is about as big as the United States. Africa also has the Nile, one of the longest rivers on Earth. It flows north through Egypt to the sea.

Africa is more than desert. It has rain forests, grasslands called savannas and snowy peaks like Mount Kilimanjaro. It also has big modern cities. Lagos in Nigeria and Cairo in Egypt each have millions of people.

lessons.title: The Empire of Mali
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, Mali in West Africa was a rich empire known for gold, trade and learning.
reading: About 700 years ago, a great *empire* ruled much of West Africa. An empire is a group of lands ruled by one leader. This was the Mali Empire. It grew rich from gold and from salt, which traders carried across the Sahara on camels.

Its most famous ruler was Mansa Musa. In 1324 he traveled to Mecca, the holy city of Islam. He brought so much gold that people talked about him for years. Cairo, a city on his way, remembered his visit long after.
The city of Timbuktu in Mali became a center of learning. Scholars there wrote and copied books about religion, law, math and the stars. Some of these old books are still kept in Timbuktu today.

lessons.title: A Day With Amina's Family
lessons.mainIdea: In Dakar, Senegal, markets, shared meals and music fill a family's day.
reading: Amina lives in Dakar, the capital of Senegal, on the Atlantic coast. Fishing boats painted in bright colors come in each morning. Her aunt buys fresh fish at the market and talks with the sellers she knows.

Many people in Senegal speak Wolof at home and French at school. French is the official language, from the years when France ruled the country. Senegal became independent in 1960. Most people in Senegal are Muslim.

At lunch, the family shares thieboudienne from one big bowl. It is a dish of fish, rice and vegetables. Guests are welcomed warmly. Senegal is proud of its *hospitality*, the custom of making visitors feel at home.

lessons.title: Indigenous Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Indigenous nations lived in the Americas for thousands of years and still live there today.
reading: Long before Europeans arrived, the Americas were home to many nations. The Maya built cities with tall stone temples. The Inca built roads through the Andes. In Illinois, people built great earth mounds at Cahokia, near today's St. Louis.

The first peoples of a place are called *Indigenous* peoples. In the Americas they spoke hundreds of languages. Each nation had its own leaders, farming, stories and beliefs. Many grew corn, beans and squash.

After Europeans came, Indigenous peoples lost much land and many lives to war and disease. But they did not disappear. Today there are 574 federally recognized tribal nations in the United States. Millions of people in Mexico, Guatemala, Peru and Bolivia speak Indigenous languages.

words.d: the first peoples to live in a place, and their descendants today
a people with its own land, leaders and way of life

lessons.title: Many Languages in the Americas
lessons.mainIdea: Because of history, people in the Americas speak Spanish, Portuguese, English, French and Indigenous languages.
reading: About 500 years ago, ships from Europe began arriving in the Americas. Spain, Portugal, England and France each set up *colonies*. A colony is land ruled by a faraway country. Enslaved Africans were also forced to come, and they shaped these lands too.

The colonies left their languages behind. Most of Central and South America speaks Spanish. Brazil speaks Portuguese. The United States and most of Canada speak English. In Quebec, in Canada, most people speak French.

Culture in the Americas is a mix. It blends Indigenous, European and African ways. Music like jazz from New Orleans and samba from Brazil grew from African roots. Foods like corn and chocolate came from Indigenous farmers.

words.d: land ruled by a country that is far away
forced to work without pay and without freedom
